I'd rethink your school argument there. It's pretty silly if you break it down. Fundamentally, you're arguing that because you were a bad student that wasting money is better (or no less bad) than spending it on education. But I do want to hit on the numbers you talked about, the 'pathetic' $40k and 1/6th of the budget spending in particular.

While bomb development does involve a number of high level position, there's not much for the average person. The manufacturing and assembly is all heavily automated. And the people at high levels are in no shortage of options. And as for the wages of whatever low level positions might exist, I have some direct experience there. My wife was offered a software development position at one of the main bomb makers in the US, Boeing. The salary was, coincidentally, exactly $40k made even worse by up front statement that there would be no holidays and no benefits offered. And software is generally going to pay substantially better than any sort of factory line type work.

Then there's the "military spending is 1/6th of our budget." I don't think this is something you'd repeat if you knew how it must have been calculated. Let me start with a quick question. Imagine congress (and the president) agreed to cut every single expenditure they could down to $0 and then allocate all of that extra money to the military. How much would the military spending increase by? If you were right, it'd be a factor of 6. The real answer is that it'd just about double.

When people refer to when they speak of the budget is what the president and congress allocate each year. This is known as discretionary spending. Military spending, as of 2016, was a shade under 50% of this budget - $580 billion in total. The rest of the budget is known as mandatory spending and cannot be changed without passing new laws. This includes things like social security, medicare, interest in our national debt, and also a variety of military related expenses such as veteran's affairs, military pensions, and so on. That "1/6th" figure was derived by looking only at the discretionary spending on military and comparing that against the entire budget - ignoring mandatory military spending. Super disingenuous stuff.

I'm actually arguing that the government has no place educating people, our technological approach in education is counterproductive and mismanaged, and that way more money is wasted on underperforming schools than on fighting our enemies.

Is every dollar we spend on the military spent well? No. I'd rather pay higher salaries and better pensions than buy crappy planes and ships that're designed to need excessive maintenance. But we need a strong military. We don't need federal funding for education, we don't need government intervention in the economy, and don't need enemy military forces alive and operable.

Without arguing the specifics of that point, I think there's a broader answer here. Waste in one department does not excuse waste in another. If you see education spending resulting in effectively lighting $100 million on fire, I'd be the first to join you in opposition to it. A department's expenditure of funds should be able to support itself, in a vacuum.
